activity.notes: Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan was acclaimed caliph in 685 as successor to Marwan I and remained Umayyad caliph until his death in 705. His accession occurred during the Second Fitna: at first his effective authority was concentrated in Syria and Egypt, while Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and other rivals controlled major regions. Campaigns in 691-692 defeated those rivals and restored Umayyad control over Iraq and the Hijaz. ATLAS therefore preserves the full 685-705 caliphal reign rather than beginning the Activity only in 692; the changing territorial reach reflects contested and subsequently consolidated control, not an interruption in Abd al-Malik's tenure as Umayyad caliph. His reign also saw major centralizing reforms, including administrative Arabization, monetary reform, and the construction of the Dome of the Rock.

sources.title: The Umayyad Empire
sources.citation_text: Andrew Marsham's Cambridge history states that Abd al-Malik was acclaimed by the Umayyad clan and Syrian supporters in 685, explains that victories in 691-692 extended his rule beyond Syria and Egypt to Iraq and the Hijaz, and treats his reign through 705.

sources.title: The Imperial Marwanid Caliphate
sources.citation_text: Cambridge's chapter on the imperial Marwanid caliphate distinguishes Abd al-Malik's 685 acclamation from the consolidation of empire-wide rule in 691-692, when loyalists regained Iraq and the Hijaz.

sources.title: Abd al Malik ibn Marwan
sources.citation_text: The Metropolitan Museum of Art identifies Abd al-Malik as the fifth Umayyad caliph and describes his centralizing institutions, monetary reform, and patronage of the Dome of the Rock.

sources.title: The Eastern Mediterranean, 500-1000 A.D. - Chronology
sources.citation_text: The Metropolitan Museum's Heilbrunn Timeline explicitly gives Abd al-Malik's reign as 685-705 and records the completion of the Dome of the Rock under his patronage in 691.
